summary: Retires and obsoletes the Tao of the IETF as an IETF-maintained document, and obsoletes RFC 6722, which described its publication process. It gives the reasons for the retirement and keeps the last version of the Tao in an appendix. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF had a guidebook for newcomers. This says the book will no longer be kept up to date, and explains why.

questions: what is the tao of the ietf
is the tao of the ietf still maintained
why was the tao of the ietf retired
subtitle: The IETF stops maintaining its newcomer guide as an RFC-era document and explains why.

tldr.problem: The Tao of the IETF, a long guide for newcomers, did not keep up with changes in IETF processes and became a commonly out-of-date source of information.
tldr.mechanism: This document formally retires the Tao as a single standalone document, obsoletes RFC 6722 (the process for publishing it as a web page), and moves the job to the IETF website. The last edition is kept in an appendix.
tldr.outcome: The Tao is no longer maintained. Newcomer information is meant to come from the IETF website instead, in shorter and more timely forms.

today: RFC 9592 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 6722 and retires the Tao of the IETF. The Tao is no longer maintained as an IETF document, and newcomer information is provided through the IETF website.

sections.title: What the Tao Was
sections.content:
The Tao of the IETF (the Tao) was first published as RFC 1391 in 1993. It described how IETF meetings and Working Groups work, discussed organizations related to the IETF, and introduced the working processes to new participants.

It was never a formal IETF process document. It was a community-developed and maintained informational overview. After 13 years as an RFC it became a web page, following the process in RFC 6722, and stayed one for over a decade.

The document says the Tao did not keep up with changes in the processes of the community and the organization, and so ceased to be a reliable source of information. RFC 9592 formally retires and obsoletes it as a single standalone document.
sections.plainLanguage: The Tao was a guidebook that told new people how the IETF works. It was a friendly guide, not an official rulebook.

sections.title: Reasons for Retirement
sections.content:
The short version: the breadth of topics, the unpredictable schedule of updates, and the high overhead of revising and reviewing the content did not match what the intended audience needed or preferred. The RFC gives three specific reasons.

  • Infrequent updates. After RFC 1391 in January 1993, four more versions were published as RFCs in the following 17 years. RFC 6722 in August 2012 was meant to let the Tao be updated more easily, yet only four additional versions appeared in the next 11 years. Reviewing and approving the whole document took considerable effort and time.
  • Unwieldy format. A large, consolidated document is a heavy investment for readers and hard for editors to keep current. The example given is the popularity of the IETF Hackathon with new participants, which prompted an update that ended up buried in an already long document.
  • Changing participation modes. The Tao was written to welcome people to in-person meetings as attendance grew with the Internet in the 1990s. Other ways in emerged over the decades, and remote participation became a much more significant part of IETF meetings, but the Tao stayed focused on in-person attendance.
sections.plainLanguage: The handbook was so long that fixing even one page meant checking the whole book. It also kept talking about showing up in person when many people now join from home.

sections.title: Going Forward
sections.content:
The content of the Tao has already been integrated into the IETF website, which is the main channel of communication for newcomers and a general audience. The RFC says the content is continuously kept up to date with a variety of media for different audiences.

It lists examples of ways to improve communication with newcomers and existing participants:

  • More focused guides, for example on IETF Hackathon participation or starting new work.
  • Alternative formats such as multiple shorter documents, on-demand video and podcasts.
  • New channels such as blog posts, an improved Datatracker and Slack.

The conclusion restates that the wide range of topics, the unpredictable update schedule and the high review overhead made the Tao hard to maintain and commonly out of date. The document calls itself the end of the road for the Tao, which is now retired.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one giant book, the IETF now spreads the help around: a website, short guides, videos and chat channels that are easier to keep fresh.

sections.title: The Archived Last Edition
sections.content:
For archival purposes, Appendix A reproduces the last edition of the Tao as published under the RFC 6722 process. The RFC notes that several links to outside resources do not work at the time of publication and that minor errors in the text were corrected.

That archived text covers what the IETF is, how IETF meetings and Working Groups run, how Internet-Drafts and RFCs are produced, how to contribute, and how the IETF relates to the outside world. The RFC itself adds nothing new to those topics.

The RFC has no security considerations and no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The old handbook is not thrown away. A copy is tucked into the back of this document so people can still read it as a keepsake.
